breaths.text: The nuptials were finished.
The rabbi let himself down into an armchair.
Then he came out of the room and saw tables set the full length of the yard.
There were so many of them that they poked their tail out through the gates onto Hospital Street.
Tables covered in velvet wound through the yard like snakes whose bellies had been laid with patches of every color, and they sang in thick voices—those patches of orange and red velvet.
The apartments had been turned into kitchens.
Through soot-blackened doors a fat flame beat, a drunken, puffy flame.
In its smoky rays old women's faces were baking, women's shaking chins, slovenly breasts.
Sweat, pink as blood, pink as the froth of a mad dog, ran over these heaps of overgrown, sweetly stinking human meat.
Three cooks, not counting the dishwashers, were preparing the wedding supper, and over them reigned eighty-year-old Reyzl, traditional as a Torah scroll, tiny and humpbacked.
Before supper a young man, unknown to the guests, slipped into the yard.
He asked for Benya Krik.
He drew Benya Krik aside.
"Listen, King," the young man said.
"I have a pair of words to say to you.
Aunt Khana from Kostetskaya sent me... "
"Well, all right," answered Benya Krik, nicknamed the King.
"What pair of words is this? "
"A new inspector arrived at the precinct yesterday, Aunt Khana told me to tell you... "
"I knew that the day before yesterday," answered Benya Krik.
"Further. "
"The inspector gathered the precinct and made the precinct a speech... "
"A new broom sweeps clean," answered Benya Krik.
"He wants a roundup.
Further... "
"And when the roundup will be, do you know, King? "
"It will be tomorrow. "
"King, it will be today. "
"Who told you this, boy? "
"Aunt Khana told it.
Do you know Aunt Khana? "
"I know Aunt Khana.
Further. "
The inspector gathered the precinct and said them a speech.
'We must strangle Benya Krik,' he said, 'because where there is a sovereign emperor, there is no king.
Today, when Krik is marrying off his sister and they will all be there, today we must make the roundup... '"
"Further. "
Then the spies began to be afraid.
They said: if we make a roundup today, when he has a feast, Benya will get angry, and much blood will go.
So the inspector said—my pride is dearer to me... "
"Well, go," answered the King.
"What to tell Aunt Khana about the roundup. "
"Tell her: Benya knows about the roundup. "
And he left, that young man.
After him went some three of Benya's friends.
They said they would return in half an hour.
And they returned in half an hour.
That is all.
They did not sit down at table by seniority.
Foolish old age is no less pitiful than cowardly youth.
Nor by wealth.
The lining of a heavy purse is sewn from tears.
At the table, in the first place, sat the bridegroom and the bride.
This is their day.
In the second place sat Sender Eichbaum, the King's father-in-law.
This is his right.
The history of Sender Eichbaum ought to be known, because this is no simple history.
How did Benya Krik, raider and king of raiders, become Eichbaum's son-in-law?
How did he become son-in-law to a man who had sixty milch cows, less one?
The whole matter is in a raid.
Only a year ago Benya wrote Eichbaum a letter.
"Monsieur Eichbaum," he wrote, "be so good as to place, tomorrow morning, under the gate at Sofievskaya, 17, twenty thousand rubles.
If you do not do this, such a thing awaits you as has not been heard of, and all Odessa will talk of you.
Respectfully, Benya the King. "
Three letters, each clearer than the last, remained without answer.
Then Benya took measures.
They came at night—nine men with long sticks in their hands.
The sticks were wound with tarred oakum.
Nine blazing stars lit up in Eichbaum's cattle yard.
Benya smashed the locks of the shed and began leading the cows out one by one.
A fellow with a knife was waiting for them.
He knocked a cow over with a single blow and plunged the knife into the cow's heart.
On the ground, flooded with blood, the torches blossomed like fiery roses, and shots thundered.
With shots Benya drove off the dairywomen who had run to the cowshed.
And after him the other raiders began shooting into the air, because if you do not shoot into the air, you can kill a person.
And so, when the sixth cow fell with a dying moan at the King's feet—then Eichbaum ran into the yard in nothing but his drawers and asked:
"What will come of this, Benya? "
"If I have no money, you will have no cows, Monsieur Eichbaum.
That's two times two. "
"Come into the premises, Benya. "
And in the premises they came to terms.
The slaughtered cows were divided between them in half.
Eichbaum was guaranteed inviolability and issued a certificate of it with a seal.
But the miracle came later.

During the raid, on that terrible night when the stabbed cows bellowed and the heifers slipped in their mothers' blood, when the torches danced like black virgins and the milk-women shied and squealed under the muzzles of friendly Brownings—on that terrible night the daughter of old Eichbaum, Tsilya, ran into the yard in a cut-work nightshirt.
And the King's victory became his defeat.
Two days later Benya, without warning, returned to Eichbaum all the money taken, and after that he appeared in the evening on a visit.
He was dressed in an orange suit; under his cuff a diamond bracelet shone; he entered the room, greeted them, and asked of Eichbaum the hand of his daughter Tsilya.
The old man was struck by a light stroke, but he rose.
There was still twenty years of life in the old man.
"Listen, Eichbaum," the King said to him, "when you die, I will bury you in the First Jewish Cemetery, right at the gates.
I will put up for you, Eichbaum, a monument of pink marble.
I will make you warden of the Brodsky Synagogue.
I will throw over the profession, Eichbaum, and enter your business as a partner.
We will have two hundred cows, Eichbaum.
I will kill all the dairymen except you.
A thief will not walk on the street where you live.
I will build you a dacha at the Sixteenth Station...
And remember, Eichbaum, you were not a rabbi in your youth either.
Who forged the will—we will not speak of this loudly?...
And your son-in-law will be a King, not a snot-nose, but a King, Eichbaum... "
And he got what he wanted, Benya Krik, because he was passionate, and passion holds dominion over the worlds.
The newlyweds lived three months in fat Bessarabia, among grapevines, abundant food, and the sweat of love.
Then Benya returned to Odessa in order to marry off his forty-year-old sister Dvoyra, who suffered from Basedow's disease.
And now, having told the history of Sender Eichbaum, we may return to the wedding of Dvoyra Krik, the King's sister.
At this wedding they served for supper turkeys, roast hens, geese, stuffed fish, and a fish soup in which lemon lakes shone with mother-of-pearl.
Over the dead goose-heads flowers swayed like lavish plumes.
But is it roast hens that the foaming surf of the Odessa sea throws up on the shore?
All that is most noble of our contraband, all for which the earth is famed from end to end, did on that starry, that blue night its destructive, its seductive work.
Wine not of this place heated the stomachs, sweetly broke the legs, stupefied the brains, and called forth a belch, sonorous as the summons of a battle trumpet.

The Black cook from the Plutarch, which had arrived the day before yesterday from Port Said, had carried beyond the customs line potbellied bottles of Jamaica rum, oily Madeira, cigars from the plantations of Pierpont Morgan, and oranges from the environs of Jerusalem.
This is what the foaming surf of the Odessa sea throws up on the shore, this is what falls sometimes to Odessa beggars at Jewish weddings.
Jamaica rum fell to them at the wedding of Dvoyra Krik, and therefore, having sucked themselves full like treyf pigs, the Jewish beggars began to pound their crutches deafeningly.
Eichbaum, his vest unbuttoned, surveyed the roaring assembly with a squinted eye and hiccupped lovingly.
The orchestra played a flourish.
It was like a divisional review.
A flourish—nothing but a flourish.
The raiders, sitting in closed ranks, were at first embarrassed by the presence of outsiders, but then they let themselves go.
Lyova Katsap smashed a bottle of vodka on the head of his beloved.
Monya the Artilleryman fired into the air.
But their rapture reached its limit when, by the custom of old times, the guests began to present gifts to the newlyweds.
The synagogue shammeses, leaping onto the tables, sang out, to the sound of the boiling flourish, the number of rubles and silver spoons given.
And here the friends of the King showed what blue blood is worth, and the still-unextinguished knighthood of Moldavanka.
With a careless movement of the hand they flung onto silver trays gold coins, rings, strands of coral.
Aristocrats of Moldavanka, they were laced into raspberry waistcoats, their shoulders were clasped by ginger jackets, and on their meaty legs the leather of heavenly azure was splitting.
Straightening to their full height and thrusting out their bellies, the bandits clapped in time to the music, shouted "Bitter!

" and threw flowers at the bride, and she, forty-year-old Dvoyra, sister of Benya Krik, sister of the King, disfigured by illness, with a swollen goiter and eyes starting from their sockets, sat on a mountain of pillows beside a puny boy, bought with Eichbaum's money and struck dumb with anguish.
The rite of gift-giving was drawing to a close, the shammeses had gone hoarse, and the double bass was not getting on with the violin.
Over the little yard a light smell of burning stretched suddenly.
"Benya," said Papa Krik, the old drayman, famed among draymen as a brute, "Benya, you know what it seems to mine?
It seems to mine our soot is burning... "
"Papa," answered the King to his drunken father, "please drink and eat, let these stupidities not agitate you... "
And Papa Krik followed his son's advice.
He ate and drank.
But the little cloud of smoke grew more and more poisonous.
Somewhere already the edges of the sky were turning pink.
And already a tongue of flame, narrow as a sword, had shot up into the height.
The guests, half-rising, began to sniff the air, and their women squealed.
The raiders then glanced at one another.
And only Benya, noticing nothing, was inconsolable.
"They are spoiling mine feast," he cried, full of despair, "dear ones, I ask you, eat and drink... "
But at that moment there appeared in the yard that same young man who had come at the beginning of the evening.
"King," he said, "I have a pair of words to say to you... "
"Well, speak," answered the King.
"You always have a pair of words in reserve... "
"King," said the unknown young man, and he giggled, "it is simply funny, the precinct is burning like a candle... "
The shopkeepers went mute.
The raiders smirked.
Sixty-year-old Manka, progenitress of the Slobodka bandits, putting two fingers in her mouth, whistled so piercingly that her neighbors rocked.
"Manya, you are not at work," Benya remarked to her.
"Colder blood, Manya... "
The young man who had brought this astonishing news was still being taken by laughter.
"They came out of the precinct, some forty men," he related, working his jaws, "and they went for the roundup; so they had gone maybe fifteen steps when it already caught fire...
Run and look, if you want... "
But Benya forbade the guests to go look at the fire.
He set off with two comrades.
The precinct was blazing properly from four sides.
Policemen, shaking their rumps, ran up the smoke-filled staircases and flung trunks from the windows.
Under cover of the noise the arrested were scattering.
The firemen were filled with zeal, but in the nearest hydrant there was no water.
The inspector—that same broom that sweeps clean—stood on the opposite sidewalk and chewed at his mustache, which was climbing into his mouth.
The new broom stood without movement.
Benya, passing the inspector, gave him a military salute.
"Good health to you, Your Honor," he said with sympathy.
"What will you say to this misfortune?
This is a nightmare... "
He stared at the burning building, shook his head, and smacked his lips:
"Ai-ai-ai... "
And when Benya returned home—in the yard the little lanterns were already going out, and in the sky the dawn was occupying.
The guests had dispersed, and the musicians dozed, their heads dropped onto the necks of their double basses.
Only Dvoyra had no intention of sleeping.
With both hands she was pushing her timid husband toward the door of their bridal chamber and looking at him carnally, like a cat that, holding a mouse in its mouth, tries it lightly with its teeth.
I began.
"Reb Arye-Leib," I said to the old man, "let us speak of Benya Krik.
Let us speak of his lightning beginning and his terrible end.
Three shadows crowd the roads of my imagination.
Here is Froim Grach.
The steel of his deeds—will it not bear comparison with the force of the King?
Here is Kolka Pakovsky.
The fury of this man contained in itself everything needful for ruling.
And did Khaim Drong truly fail to distinguish the glitter of a new star?
But why did Benya Krik alone climb to the top of the rope ladder, while all the rest hung below, on the shaky rungs? "
Reb Arye-Leib was silent, sitting on the cemetery wall.
Before us spread the green quiet of the graves.
A man who thirsts for an answer must stock himself with patience.
A man who possesses knowledge is suited by gravity.
Therefore Arye-Leib was silent, sitting on the cemetery wall. At last he said:
"Why him?
Why not them—this is what you wish to know?
Then forget awhile that spectacles sit on your nose and autumn sits in your soul.
Stop raising a row at your writing table and stuttering before people.
Picture to yourself for an instant that you raise a row in the public squares and stutter on paper.
You are a tiger, you are a lion, you are a cat.
You can pass a night with a Russian woman, and the Russian woman will remain satisfied with you.
You are twenty-five years old.
If rings were fastened to heaven and to earth, you would seize those rings and pull heaven down to earth.
And your papa is the drayman Mendel Krik.
What does such a papa think about?
He thinks about drinking a good tumbler of vodka, about giving somebody one in the mug, about his horses—and nothing more.
You want to live, and he makes you die twenty times a day.
What would you have done in Benya Krik's place?
You would have done nothing.
And he did.
Therefore he is the King, and you keep a fig in your pocket.
"He—Venchik—went to Froim Grach, who by then already looked at the world with one eye only and was what he is. He said to Froim:
"'Take me.
I want to fetch up at your shore.
The shore I fetch up at will be the winner. ' "Grach asked him:
"'Who are you, where do you come from, and what do you breathe? '
"'Try me, Froim,' answered Benya, 'and let us stop smearing white kasha on a clean table. '
"'Let us stop smearing kasha,' answered Grach.
'I will try you. '
"And the raiders gathered a council to think about Benya Krik.
I was not at this council.
But they say they gathered a council.
The eldest then was the late Levka Byk.
"'What is going on under the cap of this Venchik?
' asked the late Byk. "And one-eyed Grach gave his opinion:
"'Benya speaks little, but he speaks tasty.
He speaks little, but you want him to say something more. '
"'If that is so,' exclaimed the late Levka, 'then let us try him on Tartakovsky. '
"'Let us try him on Tartakovsky,' the council decided, and everyone in whom a conscience still lodged turned red at hearing this decision.
Why did they turn red?
You will learn of this if you go where I will lead you.
"Tartakovsky they called among us 'Jew-and-a-Half,' or else 'Nine Raids.
' 'Jew-and-a-Half' they called him because no Jew could hold in himself as much insolence and money as Tartakovsky had.
In height he stood taller than the tallest policeman in Odessa, and he had more weight than the fattest Jewess.
And 'Nine Raids' they nicknamed Tartakovsky because the firm of Levka Byk and Company had made upon his office not eight raids and not ten, but precisely nine.
To Benya, who was not yet then the King, fell the honor of performing upon Jew-and-a-Half the tenth raid.
When Froim told him of this, he said 'yes' and went out, slamming the door.
Why did he slam the door?
You will learn of this if you go where I will lead you.
"Tartakovsky has the soul of a murderer, but he is ours.
He came out of us.
He is our blood.
He is our flesh, as if one mother bore us.
Half of Odessa serves in his shops.
And he suffered through his own Moldavanka people.
Twice they kidnapped him for ransom, and once during a pogrom they buried him with choristers.
The Slobodka thugs were beating Jews then on Bolshaya Arnautskaya.
Tartakovsky ran from them and met a funeral procession with choristers on Sofiyskaya. He asked:
"'Whom are they burying with choristers? '
"Passersby answered that they were burying Tartakovsky.
The procession reached the Slobodka cemetery.
Then ours took a machine gun out of the coffin and began to pour it into the Slobodka thugs.
But Jew-and-a-Half had not foreseen this.
Jew-and-a-Half was frightened to death.
And what proprietor would not have been frightened in his place?
"A tenth raid upon a man already buried once—this was a coarse act.
Benya, who was not yet then the King, understood this better than anyone.
But he said 'yes' to Grach, and that same day he wrote Tartakovsky a letter, resembling all letters of this kind:
"Most respected Ruvim Osipovich!
Be so kind as to place by Sabbath under the rain barrel... and so forth.
In case of refusal, as you have lately begun to permit yourself, a great disappointment awaits you in your family life.
Respectfully, your acquaintance Bentsion Krik.
"Tartakovsky did not spare himself the trouble and answered without delay.
"Benya!
If you were an idiot, I would write to you as to an idiot!
But I do not know you for such, and God forbid I should know you for such.
You, it seems, are playing the boy.
Do you truly not know that this year in Argentina there is such a harvest you can choke on it, and we sit with our wheat without a start?...

And I will tell you, laying a hand on my heart, that I am sick of eating in my old age such a bitter piece of bread and living through these unpleasantnesses, after I have worked my whole life like the last dray horse.
And what have I got after these termless hard-labor works?
Ulcers, sores, troubles, and insomnia.
Drop these stupidities, Benya.
Your friend, much more than you suppose—Ruvim Tartakovsky.
"Jew-and-a-Half had done his.
He wrote a letter.
But the post did not deliver the letter to the address.
Receiving no answer, Benya got angry.
The next day he appeared with four friends at Tartakovsky's office.
Four youths in masks and with revolvers piled into the room.
"'Hands up!
' they said, and began waving pistols.
"'Work calmer, Solomon,' remarked Benya to one of those who was shouting louder than the others.
'Do not have this habit of being nervous at work'—and, turning to the clerk, white as death and yellow as clay, he asked him:
"'Is Jew-and-a-Half in the works? '
"'They are not in the works,' answered the clerk, whose surname was Muginshtein, and by name he was called Iosif, and he was the bachelor son of Aunt Pesya, a chicken-seller from Seredinskaya Square.
"'Who will be here, at last, for the boss?
' they began to interrogate the unfortunate Muginshtein.
"'I will be here for the boss,' said the clerk, green as green grass.
"'Then open us, with God's help, the cashbox!
' Benya ordered him, and an opera in three acts began.

"Nervous Solomon was packing into a suitcase money, papers, watches, and monograms; the late Iosif stood before him with raised hands, and at this time Benya was telling stories from the life of the Jewish people.
"'Once he starts playing Rothschild,' Benya said of Tartakovsky, 'then let him burn with fire.

Explain to me, Muginshtein, as to a friend: here he receives from me a business letter—why should he not sit down for five kopecks on a tram and ride over to my apartment and drink with my family a tumbler of vodka and eat whatever God has sent.
What hindered him from speaking out his soul before me?
"Benya," let him have said, "so and so, here is my balance, wait me a pair of days, let me breathe, let me spread my hands.
" What would I have answered him?
A pig does not meet a pig, but a man meets a man.
Muginshtein, have you understood me? '

"'I have understood you,' said Muginshtein, and he lied, because it was not at all clear to him why Jew-and-a-Half, a respectable rich man and a first person, should ride on a tram to eat with the family of the drayman Mendel Krik.
"And all this time misfortune was loafing under the windows like a beggar at dawn.
Misfortune burst into the office with a noise.
And though this time it had taken the form of the Jew Savka Butsis, it was drunk as a water-carrier.
"'Ho-hu-ho,' shouted the Jew Savka, 'forgive me, Venchik, I am late'—and he stamped his feet and began to wave his arms.
Then he fired, and the bullet hit Muginshtein in the belly.
"Are words needed here?
There was a man and there is no man.
An innocent bachelor lived for himself, like a bird on a branch—and now he has perished through stupidity.
A Jew looking like a sailor came and shot not into some surprise-bottle, but into the belly of a person.
Are words needed here?
"'Scram from the office,' shouted Benya, and he ran last.
But, leaving, he managed to say to Butsis:
"'I swear by my mother's coffin, Savka, you will lie next to him... '
"Now tell me, young gentleman, clipping coupons on other people's shares, how would you have acted in Benya Krik's place?
You do not know how to act.
And he knew.
Therefore he is the King, and you and I sit on the wall of the Second Jewish Cemetery and fence ourselves from the sun with our palms.
"The unfortunate son of Aunt Pesya did not die at once.
An hour after they had brought him to the hospital, Benya appeared there.
He ordered the senior doctor and the nurse called to him and said to them, without taking his hands from his cream trousers:
"'I have an interest,' he said, 'that the patient Iosif Muginshtein should recover.
I introduce myself just in case.
Bentsion Krik.
Camphor, air cushions, a private room—give with an open soul.
If not, then upon every doctor, even if he be a doctor of philosophy, there fall no more than three arshins of earth. '
"And all the same Muginshtein died that same night.
And only then did Jew-and-a-Half raise a cry through all Odessa.
"'Where does the police begin,' he howled, 'and where does Benya end? '

"'The police ends where Benya begins,' answered reasonable people, but Tartakovsky would not quiet down, and he waited until the red automobile with a musical box played on Seredinskaya Square its first march from the opera Laugh, Clown.
In broad daylight the machine flew up to the little house where Aunt Pesya lived.
"The automobile thundered with its wheels, spat smoke, shone with copper, stank of gasoline, and played arias on its signal horn.
From the automobile someone jumped out and went into the kitchen, where on the earthen floor little Aunt Pesya was thrashing.
Jew-and-a-Half sat on a chair and waved his arms.
"'Hooligan mug,' he shouted, seeing the guest, 'bandit, may the earth throw you up!
A fine fashion you have taken—to kill living people... '
"'Monsieur Tartakovsky,' answered Benya Krik in a quiet voice, 'here go the second day already that I weep for the dear departed as for a native brother.
But I know that you spit on my young tears.
Shame, Monsieur Tartakovsky—into what fireproof cabinet have you hidden shame?
You had the heart to send the mother of our departed Iosif a hundred miserable karbovanets.
My brain together with the hair stood up on end when I heard this news. '
"Here Benya made a pause.
On him was a chocolate jacket, cream trousers, and raspberry boots.
"'Ten thousand at once,' he roared, 'ten thousand at once and a pension until her death, let her live a hundred and twenty years.
And if not, then we will go out of this premises, Monsieur Tartakovsky, and sit in my automobile... '
"Then they abused each other.
Jew-and-a-Half abused Benya.
I was not at this quarrel.
But those who were, they remember.
They came together on five thousand in cash and fifty rubles monthly.
"'Aunt Pesya,' Benya then said to the disheveled old woman rolling on the floor, 'if you need my life, you can have it, but everyone makes mistakes, even God.
A tremendous mistake has come out, Aunt Pesya.
But was it not a mistake on God's side to settle Jews in Russia, so that they should suffer as in hell?
And what would have been bad if Jews lived in Switzerland, where first-class lakes, mountain air, and nothing but Frenchmen would surround them?
Everyone makes mistakes, even God.
Listen to me with your ears, Aunt Pesya.
You have five thousand in hand and fifty rubles a month until your death—live a hundred and twenty years.

The funeral of Iosif will be of the first rank: six horses like six lions, two chariots with wreaths, a choir from the Brodsky Synagogue, Minkovsky himself will come to sing over your departed son... '
"And the funeral took place the next morning.
Ask the cemetery beggars about this funeral.
Ask the shammeses from the synagogue, the sellers of kosher fowl, or the old women from the second almshouse.
Such a funeral Odessa has not yet seen, and the world will not see.
Policemen that day put on thread gloves.
In the synagogues, twined with greenery and open wide, electricity burned.
On the white horses harnessed to the chariot, black plumes swayed.
Sixty choristers walked before the procession.
The choristers were boys, but they sang with women's voices.
The wardens of the synagogue of kosher-fowl sellers led Aunt Pesya by the arms.
Behind the wardens went members of the society of Jewish clerks, and behind the Jewish clerks—sworn attorneys, doctors of medicine, and midwife-feldsheritsas.
On one side of Aunt Pesya were the chicken-sellers of the old bazaar, and on the other side were the honored dairywomen from Bugaevka, wrapped in orange shawls.
They stamped their feet like gendarmes on parade on a feast day.
From their wide hips came a smell of sea and of milk.
And behind everyone trailed the employees of Ruvim Tartakovsky.
There were a hundred of them, or two hundred, or two thousand.
On them were black frock coats with silk lapels and new boots that squealed like piglets in a sack.
"And now I will speak as the Lord spoke on Mount Sinai from the burning bush.
Put my words into your ears.
All that I saw, I saw with my own eyes, sitting here, on the wall of the second cemetery, next to lisping Moiseyka and Shimshon from the funeral office.
I saw this, I, Arye-Leib, a proud Jew living among the departed.
"The chariot drove up to the cemetery synagogue.
The coffin was set on the steps.
Aunt Pesya trembled like a little bird.
The cantor climbed out of the phaeton and began the memorial.
Sixty choristers seconded him.
And at that minute the red automobile flew out from around the turn.
It played 'Laugh, Clown' and stopped.
People were silent as the dead.
The trees were silent, the choristers, the beggars.
Four men climbed out from under the red roof and with a quiet step carried to the chariot a wreath of unseen roses.

And when the memorial was finished, four men brought their steel shoulders under the coffin and, with burning eyes and thrust-out chests, marched together with the members of the society of Jewish clerks.
"In front walked Benya Krik, whom then nobody yet called the King.
He first approached the grave, climbed onto the little mound, and stretched out his hand.
"'What do you want to do, young man?
' ran up to him Kofman from the burial brotherhood.
"'I want to say a speech,' answered Benya Krik.
"And he said a speech.
All who wished to listen heard it.
I heard it, Arye-Leib, and lisping Moiseyka, who sat on the wall beside me.
"'Gentlemen and ladies,' said Benya Krik, 'gentlemen and ladies,' he said, and the sun rose over his head like a sentry with a rifle.
'You have come to pay the last debt to an honest toiler who perished for a copper grosh.
In my name and in the name of all who are not present here, I thank you.
Gentlemen and ladies!
What did our dear Iosif see in his life?
He saw a pair of trifles.
What did he occupy himself with?
He counted other people's money.
For what did he perish?
He perished for the whole laboring class.
There are people already doomed to death, and there are people who have not yet begun to live.
And so a bullet flying into a doomed breast pierces Iosif, who in his life saw nothing but a pair of trifles.
There are people who know how to drink vodka, and there are people who do not know how to drink vodka, but drink it all the same.
And so the first receive pleasure from grief and from joy, and the second suffer for all those who drink vodka without knowing how to drink it.
Therefore, gentlemen and ladies, after we have prayed for our poor Iosif, I ask you to see to the grave an unknown to you, but already departed, Savely Butsis... '
"And, having said this speech, Benya came down from the little mound.
People were silent, the trees, and the cemetery beggars.
Two gravediggers carried an unpainted coffin to the neighboring grave.
The cantor, stuttering, finished the prayer.
Benya threw the first spadeful and went over to Savka.
After him, like sheep, went all the sworn attorneys and the ladies with brooches.
He made the cantor sing over Savka a full memorial, and sixty choristers seconded the cantor.
Savka never dreamed of such a memorial—believe the word of Arye-Leib, an old old man.
"They say that on that day Jew-and-a-Half decided to close the business.
I was not at this.
But that neither the cantor, nor the choir, nor the burial brotherhood asked money for the funeral—this I saw with the eyes of Arye-Leib.
Arye-Leib—so they call me.
And more I could not see, because the people, quietly stepping away from Savka's grave, threw themselves into running as from a fire.
They flew in phaetons, in carts, and on foot.
And only those four who had arrived in the red automobile left in it.
The musical box played its march, the machine shuddered and raced away.
"'King,' looking after it, said lisping Moiseyka, that same one who takes from me the best places on the wall.
"Now you know everything.
You know who first uttered the word 'king.
' It was Moiseyka.
You know why he did not call so one-eyed Grach, nor furious Kolka.
You know everything.
But what use, if on your nose as before sit spectacles, and in your soul autumn?... "
Froim Grach had been married once.
That was long ago; twenty years had passed since then.
The wife bore Froim a daughter then and died of the birth.
The girl they named Baska.
Her grandmother on the mother's side lived in Tulchin.
The old woman did not love her son-in-law.
She said of him: Froim by occupation is a drayman, and he has black horses, but the soul of Froim is blacker than the black coat of his horses...
The old woman did not love her son-in-law and took the newborn to herself.
She lived with the girl twenty years and then died.
Then Baska returned to her father.
This all happened so.
On Wednesday, the fifth, Froim Grach was hauling to the port, onto the steamer Caledonia, wheat from the warehouses of the Dreyfus company.
Toward evening he finished the work and drove home.
At the turn from Prokhorovskaya Street the smith Ivan Pyatirubel met him.
"Respects, Grach," said Ivan Pyatirubel.
"Some woman is hammering at your premises... "
Grach drove further and saw in his yard a woman of gigantic stature.
She had enormous hips and cheeks the color of brick.
"Papa," said the woman in a deafening bass, "the devils are already grabbing me from boredom.
I have been waiting for you the whole day...
Know that Grandmother died in Tulchin. "
Grach stood on the dray and looked at his daughter with all his eyes.
"Don't twist in front of the horses," he shouted in despair, "take the bridle of the shaft horse, you want to beat my horses for me... "
Grach stood on the wagon and waved his whip.
Baska took the shaft horse by the bridle and led the horses to the stable.
She unharnessed them and went to bustle in the kitchen.
The girl hung her father's footcloths on a line, she scoured the sooty kettle with sand, and she began to warm zrazy in an iron pot.
"You have an unbearable dirt, Papa," she said, and threw out the window the soured sheepskins lying on the floor.
"But I will drive out this dirt," Baska cried, and she gave her father supper.
The old man drank vodka from an enameled teapot and ate zrazy that smelled like a happy childhood.
Then he took his whip and went out beyond the gates.
Baska came there after him.
She had put on men's boots and an orange dress, she had put on a hat hung with birds, and she sat down on the little bench.
Evening staggered past the bench, the shining eye of sunset was falling into the sea beyond Peresyp, and the sky was red as a red number in a calendar.
All trade had already shut on Dalnitskaya, and the raiders drove toward a blind street, to the public house of Yoska Samuelson.
They rode in lacquered carriages, dressed up like hummingbirds, in colored jackets.
Their eyes were popped, one foot set out toward the running board, and in a steel outstretched hand they held bouquets wrapped in cigarette paper.
Their varnished droshkies moved at a walk; in each carriage sat one man with a bouquet, and the drivers, sticking up on the high seats, were decorated with ribbons like groomsmen at weddings.

Old Jewish women in hairpieces lazily followed the course of this habitual procession—they were indifferent to everything, the old Jewish women, and only the sons of shopkeepers and of shipwrights envied the kings of Moldavanka.
Solomonchik Kaplun, son of a grocer, and Monya the Artilleryman, son of a smuggler, were among those who tried to turn their eyes from the glitter of another's luck.
Both of them passed her, swaying like girls who have learned love; they whispered between themselves and began to move their hands, showing how they would embrace Baska if she wanted it.
And Baska wanted it at once, because she was a simple girl from Tulchin, from a self-seeking, dim-sighted little town.

She weighed five poods and several pounds more; her whole life she had lived among the spiteful growth of Podolian brokers, wandering book-peddlers, timber contractors, and she had never seen such people as Solomonchik Kaplun.
Therefore, seeing him, she began to scrape the ground with her thick legs, shod in men's boots, and said to her father.
"Papa," she said in a thunderous voice, "look at this little gentleman: he has little legs like a doll, I would strangle such little legs... "
"Ehe, Pani Grach," whispered then an old Jew sitting beside, an old Jew by the name of Golubchik, "I see your child is asking for the grass... "
"Here is a bother on my head," answered Froim to Golubchik, played with his whip, and went to himself to sleep, and he fell asleep calmly, because he did not believe the old man.
He did not believe the old man and turned out to be wrong all around.
Golubchik was right.
Golubchik occupied himself with matchmaking on our street; at night he read prayers over well-to-do departed, and he knew about life all that can be known about it.
Froim Grach was wrong.
Golubchik was right.
And indeed, from that day Baska spent all her evenings beyond the gates.
She sat on the little bench and sewed herself a dowry.

Pregnant women sat beside her; heaps of linen crawled over her splayed powerful knees; the pregnant women filled with all sorts of stuff, as a cow's udder fills on the pasture with the pink milk of spring, and at this time their husbands, one after another, came from work.
The husbands of nagging wives wrung their disheveled beards under the water tap and then yielded the place to humpbacked old women.
The old women bathed fat infants in troughs, they slapped their grandsons on shining buttocks and wrapped them in their worn skirts.
And so Baska from Tulchin saw the life of Moldavanka, our generous mother—a life stuffed with sucking infants, drying rags, and bridal nights full of suburban chic and a soldier's tirelessness.
The girl wanted such a life for herself too, but here she learned that the daughter of one-eyed Grach cannot count on a worthy match.
Then she ceased to call her father father.
"Red thief," she shouted at him in the evenings, "red thief, come to supper... "
And this continued until Baska had sewn herself six nightshirts and six pairs of drawers with lace ruffles.
Finishing the hemming of the lace, she wept in a thin voice unlike her voice, and said through tears to the unshakable Grach:
"Every girl," she said to him, "has her interest in life, and only I live like a night watchman at somebody else's warehouse.
Either do something with me, Papa, or I make an end of my life... "
Grach heard his daughter to the end, he put on a canvas burka, and the next day he went as a guest to the grocer Kaplun on Privolnaya Square.
Over Kaplun's shop a gold sign glittered.
This was the first shop on Privolnaya Square.
In it smelled of many seas and of beautiful lives unknown to us.
A boy was watering from a can the cool depth of the store and singing a song that is decent to sing only for grown-ups.

Solomonchik, the master's son, stood behind the counter; on this counter were set olives that had come from Greece, Marseilles oil, coffee in beans, Lisbon malaga, sardines of the firm Philippe et Canaud, and cayenne pepper.
Kaplun himself sat in a vest in the sun, in a little glass annex, and ate watermelon—a red watermelon with black seeds, with slanted seeds, like the eyes of sly Chinese women.
Kaplun's belly lay on the table under the sun, and the sun could do nothing with it.
But then the grocer saw Grach in the canvas burka and turned pale.
"Good day, Monsieur Grach," he said, and moved back.
"Golubchik warned me that you would come, and I have prepared for you a little pound of tea, that this is a rarity... "
And he began to talk of a new sort of tea, brought to Odessa on Dutch steamers.
Grach listened to him patiently, but then interrupted, because he was a simple man, without tricks.
"I am a simple man, without tricks," said Froim.
"I am with my horses and occupy myself with my occupation.
I give new linen with Baska and a pair of old groschen, and I myself am with Baska—whoever this is not enough for, let that one burn with fire... "
"Why should we burn?
" answered Kaplun in a patter and stroked the hand of the drayman.

"No need for such words, Monsieur Grach, for you are with us a man who can help another man, and, by the way, you can offend another man, and that you are not a Krakow rabbi, well I also did not stand under the wedding canopy with the niece of Moses Montefiore, but... but Madame Kaplun... we have a Madame Kaplun, a grandiose lady, of whom God himself will not guess what she wants... "
"And I know," interrupted Grach the shopkeeper, "I know that Solomonchik wants Baska, but Madame Kaplun does not want me... "
"Yes, I do not want you," shouted then Madame Kaplun, who had been listening at the door, and she entered the little glass annex, all blazing, with a heaving breast.
"I do not want you, Grach, as a person does not want death; I do not want you as a bride does not want pimples on her head.
Do not forget that our late grandfather was a grocer, and we must hold to our line... "
"Hold to your line," answered Grach to the blazing Madame Kaplun, and he went home to himself.

There Baska waited for him, dressed up in an orange dress, but the old man, without looking at her, spread a sheepskin under the wagons, lay down to sleep, and slept until Baska's mighty hand threw him out from under the wagon.
"Red thief," said the girl in a whisper unlike her whisper, "why must I bear your drayman manners, and why are you silent as a stump, red thief?... "
"Baska," said Grach, "Solomonchik wants you, but Madame Kaplun does not want me...
There they are looking for a grocer. "
And, fixing the sheepskin, the old man crawled under the wagons again, and Baska vanished from the yard...
All this happened on Saturday, a non-working day.
The purple eye of sunset, searching the earth, stumbled in the evening upon Grach, snoring under his dray.
A rushing ray propped itself against the sleeper with fiery reproach and led him out onto Dalnitskaya Street, which was dusty and glittering like green rye in the wind.
Tatars were walking up Dalnitskaya, Tatars and Turks with their mullahs.
They were returning from pilgrimage from Mecca to their homes in the Orenburg steppes and in Transcaucasia.
A steamer had brought them to Odessa, and they were walking from the port to the inn of Lyubka Shneyveys, nicknamed Lyubka the Cossack.
Striped unbending robes stood on the Tatars and flooded the roadway with the bronze sweat of the desert.
White towels were wound around their fezzes, and this marked a man who had bowed to the dust of the Prophet.
The pilgrims reached the corner, they turned toward Lyubka's yard, but they could not pass there, because at the gates a multitude of people had gathered.
Lyubka Shneyveys, with a purse at her side, was beating a drunken muzhik and shoving him onto the roadway.
She beat with a clenched fist on the face as on a tambourine, and with the other hand she held the muzhik so that he should not fall away.
Trickles of blood crawled on the muzhik between the teeth and near the ear; he was thoughtful and looked at Lyubka as at a stranger; then he fell on the stones and fell asleep.
Then Lyubka pushed him with her foot and returned to her shop.
Her watchman Yevzel closed the gates after her and waved a hand to Froim Grach, who was passing by...
"Respects, Grach," he said, "if you want to observe something from life, then come into our yard, there is something to laugh at... "
And the watchman led Grach to the wall where the pilgrims who had arrived the day before were sitting.
An old Turk in a green turban, an old Turk, green and light as a leaf, lay on the grass.
He was covered with a pearl sweat, he breathed hard and rolled his eyes.
"Here," said Yevzel, and he straightened the medal on his worn jacket, "here you have a life drama from the opera Turkish Sickness.
He is finishing, the old fellow, but you cannot call a doctor to him, because he who finishes on the road from the god Muhammad to his home is counted among them the first lucky man and a rich man...
Khalvash," shouted Yevzel at the dying man and burst out laughing, "here comes the doctor to treat you... "
The Turk looked at the watchman with a child's fear and hatred and turned away.
Then Yevzel, pleased with himself, led Grach to the opposite side of the yard, to the wine cellar.
In the cellar lamps were already burning and music was playing.
Old Jews with heavy beards were playing Romanian and Jewish songs.
Mendel Krik was drinking at a table wine from a green glass and telling how his own sons had crippled him—the elder Benya and the younger Levka.
He roared his story in a hoarse and terrible voice, showed his pulverized teeth, and let people feel the wounds on his belly.
Volhynian tzaddiks with porcelain faces stood behind his chair and listened in a freeze to the bragging of Mendel Krik.
They marveled at everything they heard, and Grach despised them for this.
"Old braggart," he muttered of Mendel, and ordered himself wine.
Then Froim called to himself the mistress, Lyubka the Cossack.
She was cursing at the doors and drinking vodka standing.
"Speak," she shouted at Froim, and in fury she cocked her eyes.
"Madame Lyubka," answered her Froim, and he sat her beside himself, "you are a clever woman, and I have come to you as to a native mama.
I hope in you, Madame Lyubka—first in God, then in you. "
"Speak," shouted Lyubka, ran through the whole cellar, and then returned to her place. And Grach said:
"In the colonies," he said, "the Germans have a rich harvest of wheat, and in Constantinople groceries go for half of nothing.
A pood of olives they buy in Constantinople for three rubles, and they sell them here at thirty kopecks a pound...
It has become good for grocers, Madame Lyubka, grocers walk around very fat, and if you come to them with delicate hands, a person could become happy...
But I have remained alone in my work, the late Lyova Byk has died, I have help from nowhere, and here I am alone, as God is alone in heaven. "
"Benya Krik," said then Lyubka, "you tried him on Tartakovsky, what is bad for you in Benya Krik? "
"Benya Krik?
" repeated Grach, full of astonishment.
"And he is a bachelor, it seems to me? "
"He is a bachelor," said Lyubka.
"Twist him with Baska, give him money, bring him out into people... "
"Benya Krik," repeated the old man, like an echo, like a far echo.
"I did not think of him... "
He stood up, muttering and stuttering; Lyubka ran ahead, and Froim trudged after her.
They passed into the yard and climbed to the second floor.
There, on the second floor, lived the women whom Lyubka kept for travelers.
"Our bridegroom is at Katyusha's," Lyubka said to Grach.
"Wait for me in the corridor"—and she went into the end room, where Benya Krik lay with a woman by the name of Katyusha.
"Enough of drooling," the mistress said to the young man.
"First you have to settle yourself at some business, Venchik, and then you can drool...
Froim Grach is looking for you.
He is looking for a man for work and cannot find him... "
And she told all she knew about Baska and about the affairs of one-eyed Grach.
"I will think," answered her Benya, covering with a sheet Katyusha's bare legs.
"I will think, let the old man wait for me. "
"Wait for him," Lyubka said to Froim, who had remained in the corridor.
"Wait for him, he will think... "
The mistress moved a chair up to Froim, and he sank into a boundless waiting.
He waited patiently, like a muzhik in an office.
Behind the wall Katyusha moaned and overflowed with laughter.
The old man dozed two hours, and maybe more.
Evening had long since become night, the sky had blackened, and its milky ways were filled with gold, glitter, and coolness.
Lyubka's cellar was already closed, the drunks lay in the yard like broken furniture, and the old mullah in the green turban had died toward midnight.

Then music came from the sea, French horns and trumpets from English ships; music came from the sea and died away, but Katyusha, thorough Katyusha, was still heating for Benya Krik her painted, her Russian and rosy paradise.
She moaned behind the wall and overflowed with laughter; old Froim sat without moving at her door; he waited until one in the morning and then knocked.
"Man," he said, "are you truly laughing at me? "
Then Benya at last opened the door of Katyusha's room.
"Monsieur Grach," he said, embarrassed, shining, and covering himself with a sheet, "when we are young, we think of women that this is merchandise, but this is only straw that burns from nothing... "
And, having dressed, he straightened Katyusha's bed, fluffed her pillows, and went out with the old man onto the street.
Walking, they reached the Russian cemetery, and there, by the cemetery, the interests of Benya Krik and of one-eyed Grach, the old raider, came together.
They came together on this: that Baska brings her future husband three thousand rubles of dowry, two blooded horses, and a pearl necklace.
They came together also on this: that Kaplun is obliged to pay two thousand rubles to Benya, Baska's bridegroom.

He was guilty of family pride—Kaplun of Privolnaya Square; he had grown rich on Constantinople olives; he had not spared Baska's first love, and therefore Benya Krik decided to take upon himself the task of collecting from Kaplun two thousand rubles.
"I will take this upon myself, Papa," he said to his future father-in-law.
"God will help us, and we will punish all the grocers... "
This was said at dawn, when night had already passed—and here begins a new history, the history of the fall of the house of Kaplun, a tale of its slow ruin, of arsons and of night shooting.
And all this—the fate of the arrogant Kaplun and the fate of the girl Baska—was decided on that night when her father and her sudden bridegroom walked along the Russian cemetery.
Lads were then dragging girls behind the fences, and kisses sounded on the gravestones.
In Moldavanka, at the corner of Dalnitskaya and Balkovskaya streets, stands the house of Lyubka Shneyveys.
In her house are a wine cellar, an inn, an oats shop, and a dovecote for a hundred pair of Kryukov and Nikolaev pigeons.

These shops and lot number forty-six in the Odessa quarries belong to Lyubka Shneyveys, nicknamed Lyubka the Cossack, and only the dovecote is the property of the watchman Yevzel, a retired soldier with a medal.
On Sundays Yevzel goes out onto Okhotnitskaya and sells pigeons to clerks from the city and to neighboring boys.
Besides the watchman, on Lyubka's yard live also Pesya-Mindl, cook and procuress, and the manager Tsudechkis, a little Jew resembling in height and little beard our Moldavanka rabbi, Ben Zkharya.
Of Tsudechkis I know many stories.
The first of them is the story of how Tsudechkis entered as manager at the inn of Lyubka, nicknamed the Cossack.
Some ten years ago Tsudechkis brokered for a certain landowner a threshing machine with horse drive, and in the evening he led the landowner to Lyubka in order to celebrate the purchase.
His purchaser wore whiskers beside his mustaches and walked in patent-leather boots.
Pesya-Mindl gave him for supper stuffed Jewish fish and then a very good young lady, by the name of Nastya.
The landowner spent the night, and in the morning Yevzel woke Tsudechkis, who had curled up like a bagel at the threshold of Lyubka's room.

"Here," said Yevzel, "you bragged yesterday evening that the landowner bought a threshing machine through you, so be it known to you that, having spent the night, he ran away at dawn like the very last.
Now take out two rubles for the snack and four rubles for the young lady.
It seems you are a seasoned old man. "
But Tsudechkis did not give the money.
Yevzel then shoved him into Lyubka's room and locked it with a key.
"Here," said the watchman, "you will be here, and then Lyubka will come from the quarry and, with God's help, will take the soul out of you.
Amen. "
"Convict," answered Tsudechkis to the soldier, and he began to look about in the new room.
"You know nothing, convict, except your pigeons, and I still believe in God, who will lead me out of here as He led all the Jews—first from Egypt and then from the desert... "
The little broker wanted to express much more to Yevzel, but the soldier took the key with him and left, thundering with his boots.
Then Tsudechkis turned and saw by the window the procuress Pesya-Mindl, who was reading a book, The Wonders and Heart of the Baal Shem.
She was reading a Hasidic book with a gilt edge and rocking with her foot an oak cradle.
In this cradle lay Lyubka's son, Davidka, and he was crying.
"I see fine order on this Sakhalin," said Tsudechkis to Pesya-Mindl.
"Here a child lies and is tearing himself to pieces, that this is pitiful to look at, and you, fat woman, sit like a stone in the forest and cannot give him a pacifier... "

"You give him a pacifier," answered Pesya-Mindl, without tearing herself from the book, "if only he will take from you, old deceiver, this pacifier, because he is already big as a katsap and wants only mama's milk, and his mama is galloping about her quarries, drinking tea with Jews at the inn The Bear, buying contraband in the harbor, and thinking of her son as of last year's snow... "

"Yes," said then to himself the little broker, "you are in Pharaoh's hands, Tsudechkis"—and he went to the eastern wall, muttered the whole morning prayer with additions, and then took the crying infant in his arms.

Davidka looked at him with bewilderment and waved his raspberry little legs in infant sweat, and the old man began to walk about the room and, swaying like a tzaddik at prayer, struck up an endless song.
"Ah-ah-ah," he sang, "here for all children figs, but for our Davidka kalachi, so that he should sleep by day and in the nights...
Ah-ah-ah, here for all children fists... "
Tsudechkis showed Lyubka's son a little fist with gray hairs and went on repeating about figs and kalachi until the boy fell asleep and until the sun reached the middle of the glittering sky.
It reached the middle and trembled, like a fly exhausted by the heat.

Wild muzhiks from Nerubaisk and Tatarka, who had stopped at Lyubka's inn, crawled under the wagons and fell asleep there in a wild, ringing sleep; a drunken artisan came out to the gates and, scattering his plane and saw, collapsed on the ground, collapsed and began to snore in the middle of the world, all in golden flies and the blue lightnings of July.
Not far from him, in the cool, sat wrinkled German colonists who had brought Lyubka wine from the Bessarabian border.
They lit their pipes, and the smoke from their curved stems began to tangle in the silver bristle of unshaven and old-man's cheeks.
The sun hung from the sky like the pink tongue of a thirsty dog; a gigantic sea rolled in the distance upon Peresyp, and the masts of far ships wavered on the emerald water of the Odessa gulf.
The day sat in an ornamented boat; the day was sailing toward evening, and toward evening, only in the fifth hour, Lyubka returned from the city.
She arrived on a roan little horse with a big belly and a grown-out mane.
A fellow with thick legs and in a calico shirt opened the gates for her; Yevzel held the bridle of her horse, and then Tsudechkis shouted to Lyubka from his captivity:
"Respects to you, Madame Shneyveys, and good day.
Here you went away for three years on business and threw onto my hands a hungry child... "
"Shut it, mug," answered Lyubka to the old man, and she climbed down from the saddle.
"Who is that opening his mouth in my window? "

"That is Tsudechkis, a seasoned old man," answered the soldier with a medal to the mistress, and he began to tell her the whole story with the landowner, but he did not tell it to the end, because the broker, interrupting him, squealed with all his strength.
"What a nerve," he squealed, and flung down his yarmulke.
"What a nerve to throw onto the hands a stranger's child and yourself to vanish for three years...
Go give him the tit... "
"Here I come to you, swindler," muttered Lyubka, and she ran to the stairs.
She entered the room and took a breast from her dusty blouse.
The boy reached for her, gnawed her monstrous nipple, but got no milk.
A vein swelled on the mother's forehead, and Tsudechkis said to her, shaking his yarmulke.

"You want to seize everything for yourself, greedy Lyubka; you drag the whole world to yourself as children drag a tablecloth with bread crumbs; you want the first wheat and the first grapes; you want to bake white breads in the sun's heat, and your little child, such a child as a little star, must wither without milk... "
"What milk there," shouted the woman, and she pressed her breast, "when today the Plutarch arrived in the harbor and I made fifteen versts in the heat?...
And you, you have struck up a long song, old Jew—better give the six rubles... "
But Tsudechkis again did not give the money.
He let down his sleeve, bared his arm, and stuck into Lyubka's mouth a thin and dirty elbow.
"Choke, jailbird," he said, and spat in the corner.
Lyubka held in her mouth the stranger's elbow, then took it out, locked the door with a key, and went into the yard.
There already Mr. Trottyburn was waiting for her, resembling a column of ginger meat.
Mr. Trottyburn was the senior mechanic on the Plutarch.
He had brought with him to Lyubka two sailors.
One of the sailors was an Englishman, the other was a Malay.
All three of them dragged into the yard the contraband brought from Port Said.
Their crate was heavy; they dropped it on the ground, and from the crate fell cigars tangled in Japanese silk.
A multitude of women ran to the crate, and two visiting Gypsy women, swaying and jingling, began to come around from the side.
"Away, hardtack!
" Lyubka shouted at them, and she led the seamen into the shade under the acacia.
They sat there at a table; Yevzel gave them wine, and Mr. Trottyburn unrolled his goods.
He took from the bale cigars and thin silks, cocaine and files, unstamped tobacco from the state of Virginia, and black wine bought on the island of Chios.
For every goods there was a special price; every figure they washed down with Bessarabian wine, smelling of sun and of bedbugs.
Twilight ran across the yard; twilight ran like an evening wave on a wide river, and the drunken Malay, full of astonishment, touched Lyubka's breast with a finger.
He touched it with one finger, then with all the fingers in turn.
His yellow and tender eyes hung over the table like paper lanterns on a Chinese street; he sang barely audibly and fell to the ground when Lyubka shoved him with her fist.
"Look what a well-lettered one," Lyubka said of him to Mr. Trottyburn.
"The last milk will be lost on me from this Malay, and that Jew has already eaten me up over this milk... "
And she pointed at Tsudechkis, who, standing in the window, was washing his socks.
A little lamp smoked in Tsudechkis's room; his washtub foamed and hissed; he leaned out of the window, feeling they were speaking of him, and shouted with despair.
"Help, people!
" he shouted, and waved his arms.
"Shut it, mug!
" Lyubka roared with laughter.
"Shut it. "
She threw a stone at the old man, but did not hit from the first try.
The woman then seized an empty wine bottle.
But Mr. Trottyburn, the senior mechanic, took the bottle from her, took aim, and landed it in the open window.

"Miss Lyubka," said the senior mechanic, rising, and he gathered to himself his drunken legs, "many worthy people come to me, Miss Lyubka, for goods, but I give it to no one, not to Mr. Kuninzon, not to Mr. Batyu, not to Mr. Kupchik, to no one except you, because your conversation is pleasant to me, Miss Lyubka... "
And, having established himself on his shaken legs, he took by the shoulders his sailors, one an Englishman, the other a Malay, and went to dance with them about the cooling yard.
People from the Plutarch—they danced in a deep-thoughted silence.
An orange star, having rolled to the very edge of the horizon, looked at them with all its eyes.
Then they received money, took one another by the hands, and went out onto the street, swaying as a hanging lamp sways on a ship.
From the street they could see the sea, the black water of the Odessa gulf, the toy flags on the sunken masts, and the piercing lights kindled in the spacious depths.
Lyubka saw her dancing guests as far as the crossing; she remained alone on the empty street, laughed at her thoughts, and returned home.
A sleepy fellow in a calico shirt locked the gates after her; Yevzel brought the mistress the day's takings, and she went upstairs to herself to sleep.
There Pesya-Mindl, the procuress, was already dozing, and Tsudechkis was rocking with bare little feet the oak cradle.
"How you have tormented us, shameless Lyubka," he said, and he took the child from the cradle.
"But here, learn from me, filthy mother... "
He set a fine comb against Lyubka's breast and laid the son in her bed.
The child reached for his mother, pricked himself on the comb, and began to cry.
Then the old man slipped him a pacifier, but Davidka turned away from the pacifier.
"What are you conjuring over me, old rogue?
" muttered Lyubka, falling asleep.
"Be silent, filthy mother!
" he answered her.
"Be silent and learn, may you perish... "
The child pricked himself on the comb again; he took the pacifier indecisively and began to suck it.
"Here," said Tsudechkis, and he laughed.
"I have weaned your child.
Learn from me, may you perish... "
Davidka lay in the cradle, sucked the pacifier, and blew blissful spit.
Lyubka woke, opened her eyes, and closed them again.
She saw her son and the moon forcing its way to her through the window.
The moon was jumping in black clouds like a lost calf.
"Well, all right," said then Lyubka.
"Open the door for Tsudechkis, Pesya-Mindl, and let him come tomorrow for a pound of American tobacco... "
And the next day Tsudechkis came for a pound of unstamped tobacco from the state of Virginia.
He received it and a quarter-pound of tea besides.
And a week later, when I came to Yevzel to buy pigeons, I saw a new manager in Lyubka's yard.
He was tiny, like our rabbi Ben Zkharya.
Tsudechkis was the new manager.
He remained in his new post fifteen years, and in that time I learned a multitude of stories about him.
And if I am able, I will tell them in order, because these are very interesting stories.
